metadata.title: On the Capacity of the 2-user Gaussian MAC Interfering with a P2P Link

extraction_notes.note: Numbered equation (38) kept as a claim rather than an equation: the text presents it as the treating-interference-as-noise sum capacity lower bound, justified by the preceding sentence (PP8).
Claim or remark: a one-sentence fragment asserting that the analogue of Theorem 3 holds for transmitter 2, with no argument; kept as a semi-formal claim.
The interference-regime conditions of Sections 4.1-4.3 are introduced by 'Consider'/'Suppose'; those naming a regime were made definitions, the unnamed 'Suppose that the PIMAC has' one an assumption.

Proofs of Theorems 3-5 are argued in running text before each theorem; each proof node spans from the first argumentative sentence to the 'we obtain the following theorem' sentence, excluding the regime-setting sentences and the informal restatement of Theorem 5.

The paper mixes the notations $\mathcal{C}^M$ and $\mathcal{C}_M$ for the same MAC region, and the appendix text says $M(\{2,3\},2)$ where $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,3\},2)$ is meant; statements copied as written.

Introduction restatements of the results and the cited IC capacity results (Carleial, Sato, noisy-interference sum capacity) are only mentioned, not stated, so they get no nodes; figure-only content (capacity region plots) is not extracted.

nodes.name: Multiple access channel (MAC)
nodes.statement: The multiple access channel (MAC) is a scenario where several transmitters want to deliver one message each to one receiver.
differentia: several transmitters want to deliver one message each to one receiver

nodes.name: Interference channel (IC)
nodes.statement: The interference channel (IC) is another well studied model in information theory, that is a model where two transmit-receive pairs want to communicate while causing interference to each other.
differentia: two transmit-receive pairs want to communicate while causing interference to each other

nodes.name: PIMAC (MAC interfering with a P2P link)
nodes.statement: A Gaussian 2-user multiple access channel (MAC) and a Gaussian point-to-point (P2P) channel use the same medium for their communication. They interfere with each other as shown in Figure \ref{pIMAC}. We call the resulting setup the PIMAC, whose received signals can be written as \begin{align} Y_1&=X_1+X_2+h_{31}X_3+Z_1,\\ Y_2&=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+X_3+Z_2, \end{align} where $h_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel coefficient from transmitter $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$, $X_i$ is the transmit symbol of transmitter $i$ and $Z_j$ is an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) with $Z_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian 2-user MAC plus interfering P2P link: $Y_1=X_1+X_2+h_{31}X_3+Z_1$, $Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+X_3+Z_2$ with unit-variance AWGN.

nodes.name: Power constraint $P_i$
nodes.statement: Transmitter $i$ has power constraint $P_i$ so that $\mathbb{E}[X_i^2]\leq P_i$.

nodes.name: Messages, codewords and encoding functions
nodes.statement: The transmitters encode their messages $m_i$ chosen independently from $\mathcal{M}_i=\{1,\dots,2^{nR_i}\}$ into a codeword of length $n$ symbols $X_i^n\in\mathbb{R}^n$ $$X_i^n=(X_{i,1},\dots,X_{i,n})$$ using encoding functions $f_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Message $m_i$ uniform on $\mathcal{M}_i=\{1,\dots,2^{nR_i}\}$ is encoded by $f_i$ into a length-$n$ codeword $X_i^n$.

nodes.name: Decoding functions
nodes.statement: Receiver 1 decodes $m_1$ and $m_2$ by using a decoding function $g_1$, i.e. $(\hat{m}_1,\hat{m}_2)=g(Y_1^n)$, and receiver 2 decodes $m_3$ by using a decoding function $g_2$, i.e. $\hat{m}_3=g_2(Y_2^n)$.

nodes.name: Decoding error $E_i$
nodes.statement: A decoding error $E_i$ occurs if $m_i\neq\hat{m}_i$.

nodes.name: Code and average probability of error
nodes.statement: An $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ code for the PIMAC consists of encoding functions, decoding functions, and message sets, and induces an average probability of decoding error given by \begin{align} P^{(n)}=\frac{1}{2^{nR_\Sigma}}\sum_{\vec{m}\in\mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2\times\mathcal{M}_3}P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^3E_i\right), \end{align} where $R_\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^3R_i$ and $\vec{m}=(m_1,m_2,m_3)$.
nodes.statement_short: A code is encoders, decoders and message sets; its error probability $P^{(n)}$ averages the union of decoding errors over messages.

nodes.name: Average error probability $P^{(n)}$
nodes.statement: P^{(n)}=\frac{1}{2^{nR_\Sigma}}\sum_{\vec{m}\in\mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2\times\mathcal{M}_3}P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^3E_i\right),

nodes.name: Achievable rate tuple
nodes.statement: A rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ is achievable if there exists a sequence of $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ codes such that $P^{(n)}]\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
differentia: there exists a sequence of $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ codes such that $P^{(n)}]\to0$ as $n\to\infty$

nodes.name: Capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ and sum capacity $C_\Sigma$
nodes.statement: The closure of the set of all achievable rates is the capacity region of the PIMAC denoted $\mathcal{C}$, and the sum capacity is the highest achievable sum-rate \begin{align} C_\Sigma=\max_{(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}}R_\Sigma. \end{align}

nodes.name: Sum capacity $C_\Sigma$
nodes.statement: C_\Sigma=\max_{(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}}R_\Sigma.

nodes.name: MAC $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ and its capacity region $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$
nodes.statement: We denote a multiple access channel MAC from transmitters $i\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$ with AWGN with variance $1$ by $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ and its corresponding capacity region by $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$. This region is given by \begin{equation*} \mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} R_i\geq0\ \ \forall i \in \mathcal{S}: \forall \mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\\ \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}R_i\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}h_{ij}^2P_i\right) \end{array} \right\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the Gaussian MAC from transmitter set $\mathcal{S}$ to receiver $j$ and its standard polymatroid capacity region.

nodes.name: Outer bound on the PIMAC capacity region
nodes.statement: The capacity region of the PIMAC is outer bounded by $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$$ where \begin{align*} \overline{\mathcal{C}}=\left\{ \begin{array}{lr} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:&\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)&\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)&\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)& \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)& \text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)& \text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1 \end{array}\right\}. \end{align*}
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is outer bounded by $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$: single-user and MAC bounds, plus extra MAC bounds at the cross receiver whenever the corresponding cross gain is at least 1.
nodes.label: pSILemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1 (pointer)
nodes.statement: The proof is based on arguments similar to Sato's arguments in \cite{Sato} and is given in Appendix \ref{pSILemmaProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Sato-type argument; deferred to the appendix.

nodes.name: Inner bound (decode all messages at both receivers)
nodes.statement: The capacity region of the PIMAC is inner bounded by $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\underline{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$$ where \begin{align} \underline{\mathcal{C}}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is inner bounded by $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\underline{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$$
nodes.statement_short: The intersection of the two 3-user MAC regions at receivers 1 and 2 is achievable.
nodes.label: InnerBound

nodes.name: Inner bound region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$
nodes.statement: \underline{\mathcal{C}}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2) \end{array}\right\}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Each receiver simply decodes all messages in a MAC fashion. The achievable rates must be in the intersection of $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ and $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ and the statement of the theorem follows.
nodes.statement_short: Achievability: each receiver decodes all messages as in a MAC.

nodes.name: Capacity region of the PIMAC with strong interference
nodes.statement: If the PIMAC satisfies the following conditions \begin{align} h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2&\geq1\\ h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3&\geq P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3, \end{align} then the outer bound $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the inner bound $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and hence, the capacity region of the PIMAC is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\overline{\mathcal{C}}=\underline{\mathcal{C}}. \end{align}
assumptions: If the PIMAC satisfies the following conditions \begin{align} h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2&\geq1\\ h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3&\geq P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3, \end{align}
conclusions: the outer bound $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the inner bound $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and hence, the capacity region of the PIMAC is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\overline{\mathcal{C}}=\underline{\mathcal{C}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference and a power-weighted gain condition, inner and outer bounds coincide, giving the capacity region.
nodes.label: pSITheorem

nodes.name: Capacity equals both bounds
nodes.statement: \mathcal{C}=\overline{\mathcal{C}}=\underline{\mathcal{C}}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2 (sketch)
nodes.statement: By expanding the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, and using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), it can be shown that $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ reduces to $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the result follows. Details are given in Appendix \ref{pSIProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ and simplify under the conditions to obtain $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$; details in the appendix.

nodes.name: Interpretation of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: In conclusion, if the PIMAC has strong interference, i.e. (\ref{pSI1}) is satisfied, and if (\ref{pSI2}) holds, then the capacity region of the PIMAC is the intersection of two MAC capacity regions, from all transmitters to each receiver.
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference plus (7), the capacity region is the intersection of the two MAC regions at the receivers.

nodes.name: Outer bound under strong interference
nodes.statement: Let us now consider special cases of the PIMAC with strong interference $h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2\geq1$. According to Lemma \ref{pSILemma}, any achievable rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3$ for PIMAC with strong interference must satisfy \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1). \end{align} where the remaining bounds $R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ and $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ were removed because they are already included in (\ref{SIB3})-(\ref{SIB5}).
conclusions: any achievable rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3$ for PIMAC with strong interference must satisfy

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Since $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\geq1+P_3$, then it can be shown that the bound (\ref{SIB3}) is redundant and can be removed. Thus the outer bound becomes \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} Moreover $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{12}^2P_1}{1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1). \end{align} This means that the second receiver can decode $X_1^n$ while treating $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on the achievable rates. Then by subtracting the contribution of $X_1^n$ from $Y_2^n$, and decoding $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ in a MAC fashion at the second receiver, the rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$ can be achieved. If the first receiver decodes all signals in a MAC fashion, the rate region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ can be achieved. Therefore we have the following theorem.

nodes.label: VSI31-1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: In this case, the rate restriction (\ref{SIB5}) can be replaced with \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1), \end{align} which follows since the rate upper bounds on $R_3$, $R_1+R_3$, $R_2+R_3$, and $R_1+R_2+R_3$ are all redundant given $(R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)$ and $(R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)$. Therefore, the following capacity outer bound holds \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} This outer bound can be achieved if we add one more condition on the PIMAC as we show next. If (\ref{VSI31-3}) holds then receiver 1 can decode $X_3^n$ while treating $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on $m_3$. This follows since (\ref{VSI31-3}) $\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{31}^2P_3}{1+P_1+P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align} Thus, receiver 1 can remove the contribution of $X_3^n$ from $Y_1^n$ and then decode $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ achieving $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$. Let receiver 2 decode all signals in a MAC fashion achieving the region $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$. If we have \begin{align} h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3), \end{align} then the bound on $R_1+R_2+R_3$ in $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ becomes redundant and can be removed. This follows since \begin{align} &h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3)\Rightarrow\\ &\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\nonumber\\ &\hspace{5cm}+\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align} Thus, under condition (\ref{VSI31-4}) and given $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ we can replace $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ by \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)\\ (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2). \end{align} Now, since the region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ is larger than $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, we obtain the following theorem.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: Clearly, the following outer bound holds for the PIMAC \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} This outer bound can be achieved under the given conditions (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}) by decoding interference first at each receiver while treating the desired signal as noise, and then decoding the desired signal after removing the contribution of interference. Thus, as if interference is not present, the capacity region of the pIMAC becomes as given in the following theorem.

nodes.name: Genie-aided sum capacity upper bound
nodes.statement: The sum capacity of the PIMAC is upper bounded by $\overline{C}_\Sigma$, i.e. $$C_\Sigma\leq\overline{C}_\Sigma$$ where \begin{align} \overline{C}_\Sigma&\triangleq\min_{\substack{|\rho_1|,|\rho_2|\leq1,\\ \eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2,\\ \eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2}} I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G}) \end{align} with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$, $Y_{iG}$ is the corresponding channel output when the input is $X_{iG}$ and \begin{align} S_{1G}&=h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1\\ S_{2G}&=h_{31}X_{3G}+\eta_2W_2, \end{align} where $W_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that $\mathbb{E}[W_iZ_i]=\rho_i$.
assumptions: with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$, $Y_{iG}$ is the corresponding channel output when the input is $X_{iG}$
conclusions: The sum capacity of the PIMAC is upper bounded by $\overline{C}_\Sigma$, i.e. $$C_\Sigma\leq\overline{C}_\Sigma$$
nodes.statement_short: $C_\Sigma$ is at most the minimum over genie parameters of the Gaussian-input mutual informations with genie signals $S_{1G}$, $S_{2G}$.
nodes.label: SumCapacityUpperBound

nodes.name: Definition of $\overline{C}_\Sigma$
nodes.statement: \overline{C}_\Sigma&\triangleq\min_{\substack{|\rho_1|,|\rho_2|\leq1,\\ \eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2,\\ \eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2}} I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G})

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6 (sketch)
nodes.statement: We use a genie aided approach similar to \cite{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} to bound $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$. After adding the bounds, we observe that their sum is maximized by Gaussian inputs and we obtain the upper bound. Details are given in Appendix \ref{SumCapacityUpperBoundProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided bounds on $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$, then Gaussian inputs maximize the sum; details in the appendix.

nodes.name: Justification of the lower bound (38)
nodes.statement: A trivial sum capacity lower bound is obtained by using Gaussian codes and treating interference as noise.
nodes.statement_short: Achievability with Gaussian codes, treating interference as noise.

nodes.name: Treating-interference-as-noise sum capacity lower bound
nodes.statement: C_\Sigma\geq\underline{C}_\Sigma&=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_1+P_2}{1+h_{31}^2P_3}\right)\nonumber\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_3}{1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2}\right).
nodes.statement_short: Sum of single-user rates treating interference as noise lower bounds $C_\Sigma$.
nodes.label: CS_LB

nodes.name: Numerical near-tightness of the sum capacity bounds
nodes.statement: In Figure \ref{Figure:SumCapacity}, we plot the upper bound $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ and the lower bound $\underline{C}_\Sigma$ as a function of SNR, the ration between the transmit power and the noise variance, for an IMAC with $P_1=P_2=P_3=P$, $h_{12}=h_{31}=0.2$, and $h_{22}=0.1$. Notice that this upper bound is nearly tight up to some value of SNR. Intuitively, this means that below some threshold value of the interference power, treating interference as noise achieves sum rate very close to the sum capacity $C_\Sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Numerically, the upper bound is nearly tight at low SNR, so treating interference as noise is near-optimal for weak interference.

nodes.name: Sum capacity in the symmetric case $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$
nodes.statement: In the special case of $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$, then the PIMAC becomes similar to a 2-user IC with transmit signals $X_1^n+X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$. In this case, the bounds $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ in Theorem (\ref{SumCapacityUpperBound}) and $\underline{C}_\Sigma$ in (\ref{CS_LB}) coincide if $|h|(1+h_{31}^2P_3)+|h_{31}|(1+h^2(P_1+P_2))\leq1$.
nodes.statement_short: With $h_{12}=h_{22}$ the PIMAC acts like a 2-user IC and the bounds coincide under a noisy-interference condition.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Clearly, for any achievable rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$, the rate $R_3$ is upper bounded by the interference free capacity of the P2P channel, and the rate couple $(R_1,R_2)$ is included in the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$, i.e. \begin{align} R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2\},1). \end{align} Now we derive the other bounds. A genie gives $m_2$ as additional information to the second receiver. The obtained genie aided channel has a larger capacity region than the original PIMAC and can be used to outer bound $\mathcal{C}$. Now consider a rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ in the capacity region of the genie aided channel. This means that the first receiver and the second receiver are able to decode $(m_1,m_2)$ and $m_3$ reliably respectively. Since the second receiver is able to decode $m_3$, and since it knows $m_2$ from the genie, then it is able to construct \begin{align} \tilde{Y}_1^n&=\frac{Y_2^n-h_{22}X_2^n-X_3^n}{h_{12}}+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n\nonumber\\ &=X_1^n+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n+\frac{1}{h_{12}}Z_2^n \end{align} If $h_{12}^2\geq1$, then $\tilde{Y}_1^n$ is a less noisy version of $Y_1^n$. So if the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ then so does the second receiver. Thus $(R_1,R_3)$ is contained in the MAC region of $M(\{2,3\},2)$, i.e. \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,3\},2) \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1. \end{align} Similarly, we can show that \begin{align} (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{2,3\},2) &\text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1. \end{align} Finally, for any rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}$, the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ and $m_2$ reliably. Thus, if $h_{31}^2\geq1$, receiver 1 can construct a less noisy version of $Y_2^n$ and then decode $m_3$ reliably leading to the bound \begin{align} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2,3\},1) &\text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1. \end{align} and the statement of the Lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Interference-free bounds, then a genie giving $m_2$ to receiver 2 so it can build a less noisy version of $Y_1^n$ when $h_{12}^2\ge1$; symmetric arguments give the other MAC bounds.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region \begin{align*} R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\ R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\ &\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\}) \end{align*} Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to \begin{align*} R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3). \end{align*} Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ into rate constraints, simplify with (6)-(7), and match the expansion of $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$.

nodes.statement: n(R_1+R_2-\epsilon_{1n})&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;S_1^n)+I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n|S_1^n)\nonumber\\ &=h(S_1^n)-h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)+h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)\nonumber\\ &\quad-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n).
nodes.label: Q1

nodes.name: Chain rule expansion (50)
nodes.statement: n(R_3-\epsilon_{2n})&\leq h(S_2^n)-h(S_2^n|X_3^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)\nonumber\\ &\quad-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n).
nodes.label: Q2

nodes.name: Outer bound simplifies
nodes.statement: Since $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\geq1+P_3$, then it can be shown that the bound (\ref{SIB3}) is redundant and can be removed. Thus the outer bound becomes \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Constraint (9) is redundant, so the outer bound reduces to (15).

nodes.name: Receiver 2 can decode $X_1$
nodes.statement: Moreover $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{12}^2P_1}{1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1). \end{align} This means that the second receiver can decode $X_1^n$ while treating $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on the achievable rates.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Condition (12) lets receiver 2 decode $X_1^n$ treating the rest as noise at no rate cost.

nodes.name: Successive decoding at receiver 2
nodes.statement: Then by subtracting the contribution of $X_1^n$ from $Y_2^n$, and decoding $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ in a MAC fashion at the second receiver, the rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$ can be achieved.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Cancel $X_1^n$ and MAC-decode $X_2^n,X_3^n$ to achieve $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$.

nodes.name: Receiver 1 decodes all; conclude
nodes.statement: If the first receiver decodes all signals in a MAC fashion, the rate region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ can be achieved. Therefore we have the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Receiver 1 MAC-decodes all signals; the outer bound is achieved.

nodes.name: Replace constraint (11)
nodes.statement: In this case, the rate restriction (\ref{SIB5}) can be replaced with \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1), \end{align} which follows since the rate upper bounds on $R_3$, $R_1+R_3$, $R_2+R_3$, and $R_1+R_2+R_3$ are all redundant given $(R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)$ and $(R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Under (20) the bounds involving $R_3$ in (11) are redundant, leaving (21).

nodes.name: Resulting outer bound
nodes.statement: Therefore, the following capacity outer bound holds \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: State the simplified outer bound (22).

nodes.name: Receiver 1 decodes $X_3$ first
nodes.statement: This outer bound can be achieved if we add one more condition on the PIMAC as we show next. If (\ref{VSI31-3}) holds then receiver 1 can decode $X_3^n$ while treating $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on $m_3$. This follows since (\ref{VSI31-3}) $\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{31}^2P_3}{1+P_1+P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align} Thus, receiver 1 can remove the contribution of $X_3^n$ from $Y_1^n$ and then decode $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ achieving $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Condition (20) lets receiver 1 decode and cancel $X_3^n$, achieving $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$.

nodes.name: Receiver 2 MAC-decodes; sum-rate bound redundant
nodes.statement: Let receiver 2 decode all signals in a MAC fashion achieving the region $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$. If we have \begin{align} h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3), \end{align} then the bound on $R_1+R_2+R_3$ in $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ becomes redundant and can be removed. This follows since \begin{align} &h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3)\Rightarrow\\ &\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\nonumber\\ &\hspace{5cm}+\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: With receiver 2 MAC-decoding, condition (24) makes its sum-rate bound redundant.

nodes.name: Replace 3-user MAC constraint
nodes.statement: Thus, under condition (\ref{VSI31-4}) and given $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ we can replace $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ by \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)\\ (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2). \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ by the three pairwise constraints (27)-(29).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now, since the region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ is larger than $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, we obtain the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: The pair constraint at receiver 2 is looser, so the achievable region equals the outer bound.

nodes.name: Interference-free outer bound
nodes.statement: Clearly, the following outer bound holds for the PIMAC \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: The interference-free region (33) is an outer bound.

nodes.name: Achievability by decoding interference first
nodes.statement: This outer bound can be achieved under the given conditions (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}) by decoding interference first at each receiver while treating the desired signal as noise, and then decoding the desired signal after removing the contribution of interference.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: Decode interference first, cancel it, then decode desired signals.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, as if interference is not present, the capacity region of the pIMAC becomes as given in the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: Capacity equals the interference-free region.

nodes.name: Interference-free bounds
nodes.statement: Clearly, for any achievable rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$, the rate $R_3$ is upper bounded by the interference free capacity of the P2P channel, and the rate couple $(R_1,R_2)$ is included in the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$, i.e. \begin{align} R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2\},1). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $R_3$ and $(R_1,R_2)$ are bounded by their interference-free capacities.

nodes.name: Genie gives $m_2$ to receiver 2
nodes.statement: Now we derive the other bounds. A genie gives $m_2$ as additional information to the second receiver. The obtained genie aided channel has a larger capacity region than the original PIMAC and can be used to outer bound $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a genie-aided channel whose capacity region contains $\mathcal{C}$.

nodes.name: Receiver 2 constructs $\tilde{Y}_1^n$
nodes.statement: Now consider a rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ in the capacity region of the genie aided channel. This means that the first receiver and the second receiver are able to decode $(m_1,m_2)$ and $m_3$ reliably respectively. Since the second receiver is able to decode $m_3$, and since it knows $m_2$ from the genie, then it is able to construct \begin{align} \tilde{Y}_1^n&=\frac{Y_2^n-h_{22}X_2^n-X_3^n}{h_{12}}+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n\nonumber\\ &=X_1^n+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n+\frac{1}{h_{12}}Z_2^n \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Having decoded $m_3$ and knowing $m_2$, receiver 2 forms $\tilde{Y}_1^n$.

nodes.name: Bound on $(R_1,R_3)$
nodes.statement: If $h_{12}^2\geq1$, then $\tilde{Y}_1^n$ is a less noisy version of $Y_1^n$. So if the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ then so does the second receiver. Thus $(R_1,R_3)$ is contained in the MAC region of $M(\{2,3\},2)$, i.e. \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,3\},2) \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: If $h_{12}^2\ge1$, receiver 2 can also decode $m_1$, giving $(R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,3\},2)$.

nodes.name: Bound on $(R_2,R_3)$
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that \begin{align} (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{2,3\},2) &\text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric argument for $(R_2,R_3)$.

nodes.name: Bound at receiver 1 and conclusion
nodes.statement: Finally, for any rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}$, the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ and $m_2$ reliably. Thus, if $h_{31}^2\geq1$, receiver 1 can construct a less noisy version of $Y_2^n$ and then decode $m_3$ reliably leading to the bound \begin{align} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2,3\},1) &\text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1. \end{align} and the statement of the Lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: If $h_{31}^2\ge1$ receiver 1 can decode $m_3$ too; all bounds of the lemma hold.

nodes.name: Expand the inner bound
nodes.statement: We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region \begin{align*} R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\ R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\ &\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\}) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ as explicit min-type rate constraints.

nodes.name: Simplify using (6)-(7)
nodes.statement: Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to \begin{align*} R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The conditions resolve each minimum.

nodes.name: Match the outer bound
nodes.statement: Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The outer bound expands to the same constraints, so the regions coincide.

nodes.name: Define genie signals
nodes.statement: Consider the following signals \begin{align} S_1^n&=h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n\\ S_2^n&=h_{31}X_3^n+\eta_2W_2^n \end{align} where $\eta_i\in\mathbb{R}$ and $W_i^n$ is an i.i.d. sequence with $W_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that $\mathbb{E}[W_iZ_i]=\rho_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce correlated genie signals $S_1^n$, $S_2^n$.

nodes.name: Genie provides side information
nodes.statement: A genie gives these signals as extra information to the receivers. Thus, receiver $i$ knows both $Y_i^n$ and $S_i^n$ and uses them for decoding.
nodes.statement_short: Each receiver gets its genie signal.

nodes.name: Fano's inequality
nodes.statement: Using Fano's inequality, we have \begin{align} n(R_1+R_2)&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n,S_1^n)+n\epsilon_{1n}\\ nR_3&\leq I(X_3^n;Y_2^n,S_2^n)+n\epsilon_{2n} \end{align} where $\epsilon_{1n},\epsilon_{2n}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Fano bounds on $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$.

nodes.name: Chain rule for $R_1+R_2$
nodes.statement: Using the chain rule, we can write \begin{align} n(R_1+R_2-\epsilon_{1n})&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;S_1^n)+I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n|S_1^n)\nonumber\\ &=h(S_1^n)-h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)+h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)\nonumber\\ &\quad-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the mutual information into differential entropies.

nodes.name: Chain rule for $R_3$
nodes.statement: Similarly \begin{align} n(R_3-\epsilon_{2n})&\leq h(S_2^n)-h(S_2^n|X_3^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)\nonumber\\ &\quad-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Same expansion for $R_3$.

nodes.name: Goal: Gaussian inputs maximize
nodes.statement: The next step is to show that sum of the above quantities (\ref{Q1}) and (\ref{Q2}) are maximized when $X_i^n$ is i.i.d. Gaussian for all $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, i.e. $X_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i^*)$ where $P_i^*\leq P_i$. We will denote that Gaussian $X_i$ as $X_{iG}$ and the corresponding outputs as $Y_{iG}$ and $S_{iG}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing i.i.d. Gaussian inputs maximize the sum.

nodes.name: Gaussian maximizes conditional entropy
nodes.statement: Since the Gaussian distribution maximizes the conditional differential entropy under a covariance constraint, we have \begin{align} h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)&\leq nh(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})\\ h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)&\leq nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G}). \end{align} Furthermore, the terms $h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)$ and $h(S_2^n|X_3^n)$ are independent of the distribution of $X_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Max-entropy bounds on the conditional terms; noise terms are distribution-free.

nodes.name: Bound the cross difference
nodes.statement:
Now, we jointly maximize the difference $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ as follows  egin{align} &\hspace{-1cm}h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)
onumber\ &=h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n|W_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(a)}{=}h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+V_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq}nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1)
onumber\ &\quad-nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+V_2)\ &=nh(S_{1G})-nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G},X_{3G},X_{4G}), \end{align} where $(a)$ follows from \cite[Lemma 6]{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} with $V_2^n$ being an i.i.d. Gaussian sequence with $V_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1-ho_2^2)$ and $(b)$ from the worst case noise \cite{DiggaviCover} such that $\eta_1^2\leq 1-ho_2^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Annapureddy-Veeravalli Lemma 6 and worst-case noise to bound $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ by its Gaussian value.

nodes.name: Monotonicity in powers
nodes.statement: Since $\eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2$, (\ref{T1}) can be shown to be increasing in $P_1^*$ and $P_2^*$ and thus is maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Similarly, if $\eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2$, $h(S_2^n)-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n)$ can be shown to be maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Moreover, $h(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})$ and $h(Y_{2G}|S_{2G})$ can be shown to be increasing in $P_i^*$ and thus also maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: All terms increase in the input powers, so full power is optimal.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: As a result, by letting $n\to\infty$ \begin{align} &R_1+R_2+R_3\nonumber\\ &\quad\leq I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G}) \end{align} with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$ and $\eta_i\leq1-\rho_j^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Letting $n\to\infty$ gives the sum-rate bound.
